description: Ordinary formulas: intercepts, numeric and categorical predictors, level order, contrasts with explicit reference levels, centring, the response and its declared event level or trials, weights, quoted names, NFC and white space.

cases.description: One numeric predictor with the implicit intercept.
An explicit intercept gives the same IR as ordinary-01.
'0 +' removes the intercept.
'- 1' removes the intercept, giving the same IR as ordinary-03.
The intercept alone.
'0' with only a random term leaves the fixed part without columns.
The last intercept term wins: '0 + x + 1' keeps the intercept.
A one-sided formula has no response.
Levels of an undeclared string column come from the table in code-point order, so 'B' comes before 'a'. The first level is the reference.
Declared categories give the level order, before any other order.
Sum coding with an explicit reference level, which takes -1 in every column.
Simple coding of three levels: (k - 1)/k for the column's level and -1/k otherwise, so that two levels give -0.5 and 0.5.
Simple coding of two levels with the second level as reference.
A boolean column is categorical with the levels false and true, false first.
A boolean column with true as the reference level.
Declared integer categories make a numeric column categorical, with integer levels in declared order.
Mean centring over the design sample, rounded to the default 6 significant digits.
Mean centring with 2 significant digits: the mean 0.125 of the design sample rounds half to even, to 0.12. The row with a missing predictor leaves the design sample.
Mean centring before the data are seen stores the rule and its digits, not a constant.
Centring at a value that the caller gives.
log() of the response.
Quoted names hold any characters other than the backquote, the backslash and control characters. Term names quote them again.
A name in the formula is compared with the columns after NFC: the decomposed spelling in the formula names the precomposed column.
White space of every allowed kind, or none, gives the same IR as 'y ~ x + z'.
The same formula as ordinary-24, written plainly.
A binary outcome with a declared event level: the IR records the event level.
A binomial outcome with a declared trials column: the IR records the trials column.
Precision weights named by the caller.
Labels equal after NFC are one level, written in NFC.

The reference level A has rows only where x is missing. The levels still come from the table, so the reference stays A, and in the design sample the columns of B and C sum to a constant, so the sequential rule drops the later one.
A declared level that never occurs gives a column of zeros, which the sequential rule drops.
A declared date column can be a grouping factor.
The example of ir.md (The IR document): a declaration without data and simple coding.
The significant digits of a centring value are those of its decimal string, from the first to the last non-zero digit, so '100' has 1.
A data column whose name is decomposed is matched by its NFC form, and the IR writes the name in NFC, giving the same IR as ordinary-23.
A cluster unit may be a categorical predictor: only columns that identify persons are refused.
A sample column that the IR does not otherwise read also removes rows with a missing value from the design sample, and the IR lists it.
A sample column that the IR already reads is left out, giving the same IR as ordinary-01.
With missingValues [], the empty string is a level: it comes first in code-point order, names the column 'cond[]' when it is not the reference and labels a level of a grouping factor.
